newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Lev-mark peg seen enlivening Bulgarian mark trade.
newsitem.headline: Lev-mark peg seen enlivening Bulgarian mark trade.

text.p: Pegging the Bulgarian lev to the mark under a currency board would bring an increase in trade in marks on a market currently dominated by the dollar, dealers said on Thursday.
Currently the US dollar constitutes around 43-45 percent of total foreign currency turnover on the domestic forex market, central bank figures show.

"If the lev is pegged to the mark, the latter will have the status the dollar has now. The exchange rate of other foreign currencies to the lev will be determined according to their exchange rates against the mark on the international forex markets," a commercial bank dealer said.
At present, the lev/mark exchange rate is set according to the lev/dollar rate and the international dollar/mark exchange rate.
The average local market share of the mark has been up to 10 percent of daily interbank turnover this week, up from around two to three percent in the previous week, central bank figures show.
"But this was a result of the German mark's strengthening on the international markets, which made trade there much more exciting than on the local one," another dealer said.
Domestic interbank forex trade has been relatively thin and rangebound around 1,500 levs per dollar for more than a month.

Demand for marks has not risen on the local market after officials suggested that the lev should be pegged to the mark rather than the dollar at the introduction of a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime.
Under the mechanism, levs in circulation must be exactly matched by central bank reserves, imposing strict monetary discipline on the government.

"In fact it does not make such a big difference for investors to which foreign currency the lev will be pegged. If the lev is fixed at 1,000 per mark the dollar will cost around 1,700 levs, and the reverse," a third dealer said.

Bulgaria's Financial Stabilisation Council (FSC) at the start of May proposed pegging the lev to the mark rather than the dollar, citing a need to adjust to a new economic cycle compatible with Bulgaria's geopolitical and economic ties.
Germany is Bulgaria's biggest trade partner and investor.

Traditionally the dollar has been perceived as benchmark of stability as Bulgarians convert their savings mostly into dollars. The bulk of Bulgaria's $9.6 billion foreign debt is also denominated in dollars.
But the dollar is relatively strong at the moment, and a peg to the U.S. currency could make the lev NON-COMPETITIVE compared to its trading partners within a few months.
